sources.apa_citation: Anderson, K. J., & Pierce, D. A. (2009). Officiating bias: The effect of foul differential on foul calls in NCAA basketball. Journal of Sports Sciences, 27(7), 687–694. https://doi.org/10.1080/02640410902729733
sources.full_text_access: Author manuscript downloaded and methods, results, discussion read; manuscript pagination differs from published article.
evidence_locations: Manuscript PDF pp. 8–11: hypotheses and methods; 365 games, first-half restriction, logistic specifications.
Manuscript PDF pp. 11–13 and Tables 1–2 on PDF pp. 22–23: results.
Manuscript PDF pp. 13–17: discussion and player-behavior alternative.
sources.method_and_sample: Observational analysis of 365 NCAA men’s games in 2004–05: 272 conference home games and 93 neutral games. First-half fouls only to reduce intentional-fouling confounding. Binomial-independence comparison and logistic models of which team receives the next foul, controlling score/lead and conference; reports sensitivity to clustering by game.
sources.actual_findings: More accumulated fouls on a team predicted a lower probability that the next foul was called against it. Home-game net-foul coefficient −0.1180 and marginal effect −0.0295; neutral-game coefficient −0.1469. Both models have pseudo-R² below .02. Leading and visiting teams were also more likely to receive the next foul.
sources.limitations: Recorded calls do not reveal true infractions or officiating intent; changing aggression/strategy remains an alternative. NCAA first halves from one season do not establish NBA effects. This models next called foul conditional on a foul occurring, rather than the next possession’s foul probability.
sources.relevance_to_wmi: Provides the closest foul-history predecessor and motivates foul differential and score controls. WMI must distinguish balancing across teams from persistence on the same defending team and cannot convert association into proof of make-up calls.
sources.indigo_annotation: Using first-half foul sequences from 365 NCAA games, Anderson and Pierce found that the team with fewer accumulated fouls was more likely to receive the next call after accounting for score and venue. This supplies a direct precedent for examining foul history and suggests testing cumulative foul differential alongside WMI’s recent-history measures. Its low explanatory power, college sample, and inability to observe true infractions limit causal interpretations and make an NBA possession-based extension useful.

sources.apa_citation: Gong, H. (2022). The effect of the crowd on home bias: Evidence from NBA games during the COVID-19 pandemic. Journal of Sports Economics, 23(7), 950–975. https://doi.org/10.1177/15270025211073337
sources.full_text_access: Published full text downloaded from Rice institutional repository and methods, results, discussion, conclusion read.
evidence_locations: Published pp. 955–962: methodology, L2M sample, models, clustering, Table 3.
Published pp. 963–968: home/fan effects and interaction models.
Published pp. 969–971: discussion, conclusion, external-validity limits.
sources.method_and_sample: 30,695 foul actions from 1,679 qualifying NBA regular-season games, 2017–18 through 2020–21; excludes neutral bubble games. Separates incorrect calls from incorrect non-calls using league reviews. Linear probability models with home/fan interaction, team/referee and calendar fixed effects, game-clustered errors; compares crowds with empty arenas.
sources.actual_findings: No evidence that crowd presence changes home-versus-away treatment overall in this close-game sample. Fans associated with a 2.3 percentage-point increase in missed offensive-foul calls, while home players had 2.4 percentage points more missed loose-ball fouls; subgroup findings do not generalize to all foul categories.
sources.limitations: Close games and final two minutes/OT only; regular-season scope; no-fan games all from pandemic season and league review is the correctness benchmark. Observational pandemic comparison cannot fully isolate every simultaneous change. A non-significant interaction is not proof that crowds never matter.
sources.relevance_to_wmi: Supports home status and game context as controls while showing why foul type and called/non-called denominator matter. Counters a blanket referee-bias narrative and limits transfer from L2M samples to all-game WMI.
sources.indigo_annotation: Gong analyzed 30,695 reviewed foul actions from 1,679 NBA games, using pandemic empty arenas to examine crowd effects and separating incorrect calls from missed calls. The study found no overall crowd-driven difference in treatment of home and away teams, although specific foul categories showed differences. I will use it to justify venue and foul-type controls and to explain why WMI’s recorded-call patterns cannot establish referee error across an entire game.

sources.apa_citation: Deutscher, C. (2015). No referee bias in the NBA: New evidence with leagues’ assessment data. Journal of Sports Analytics, 1(2), 91–96. https://doi.org/10.3233/JSA-150012
sources.full_text_access: Full publisher PDF read through web tool; local download blocked.
sources.method_and_sample: 113 close 2014–15 games after March 1; 1,229 reviewed events, with logit analysis restricted to 619 genuine fouls.
sources.actual_findings: No support for home, superstar, or nationality bias; weak underdog preference.
sources.limitations: Small selected late-game sample; league reviewers may be biased; excludes false-positive calls from regression.
sources.relevance_to_wmi: Correctness labels are needed to evaluate bias; observed call frequency alone is insufficient.
sources.indigo_annotation: Deutscher modeled whether referees called league-confirmed fouls in 113 close NBA games. Results generally did not support the tested biases, while sample selection and league self-review restricted interpretation. I will use this counterevidence to distinguish WMI’s descriptive call patterns from claims about referee intent or accuracy.

sources.apa_citation: Gift, P. (2015). Sequential judgment effects in the workplace: Evidence from the National Basketball Association. Economic Inquiry, 53(2), 1259–1274. https://doi.org/10.1111/ecin.12186
sources.full_text_access: Abstract-only supplementary source; full text not obtained; does not count as completed full-text analysis.
sources.method_and_sample: Observational NBA offensive-foul/violation analysis; tests player-behavior explanations. Exact sample and specification [uncertain].
sources.actual_findings: Abstract reports increased scrutiny of the opposing team following a potentially questionable call; findings for the original violating team inconclusive.
sources.limitations: Full methods unavailable [uncertain]; abstract cannot establish effect size or robustness.
sources.relevance_to_wmi: Direct sequential-decision precedent, but offensive turnovers differ from defensive-foul WMI.
sources.indigo_annotation: Gift investigates whether earlier NBA offensive-foul and violation decisions influence later judgments. The abstract reports evidence consistent with greater scrutiny of the opposing team after a potentially questionable decision. This is relevant background for WMI, but it remains supplementary until the full text can be checked.

sources.apa_citation: Price, J., Remer, M., & Stone, D. F. (2012). Subperfect game: Profitable biases of NBA referees. Journal of Economics & Management Strategy, 21(1), 271–300. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1530-9134.2011.00325.x
sources.full_text_access: Publisher abstract-only supplementary source; unverified third-party manuscript not used as primary full-text analysis.
sources.method_and_sample: Compares discretionary and less discretionary turnovers as a player-behavior control. Exact published sample [uncertain].
sources.actual_findings: Abstract reports evidence favoring home teams, teams trailing within games, and teams trailing in playoff series.
sources.limitations: Full robustness and identification assumptions [uncertain]; turnover categories do not directly identify defensive-foul bias.
sources.relevance_to_wmi: Motivates negative controls and distinguishing player behavior from officiating.
sources.indigo_annotation: Price and colleagues compare turnover categories with differing referee discretion to investigate NBA officiating patterns. Their abstract reports advantages for home teams and teams trailing in games or playoff series. I will use the identification idea to motivate controls, while treating this source as preliminary until its full methods and results are available.
